# Architecture Decision Log — Game Top-Up Reseller Platform

Immutable record of foundation decisions made before any code was written. Each entry is *why*, not *what* — the living spec lives in [`prd.md`](./prd.md), the security checklist derived from these decisions lives in [`foundation-security.md`](./foundation-security.md).

**Do not edit past entries to reflect new thinking.** If a decision changes later, add a new entry that supersedes it and say so explicitly — the history of *why we changed our minds* is as valuable as the original rationale.

---

## ADR-001 (D1): Payment gateway — Xendit

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-23

**Decision:** MVP uses Xendit's standard Invoice/Payment API only (single merchant account, platform collects 100% of payment). **xenPlatform** (sub-account fund-splitting) is deferred to Phase 2.

**Rationale:** Xendit confirmed available in Malaysia (FPX, DuitNow QR, cards) with xenPlatform available for future marketplace-style splitting once real third-party resellers are onboarded with automatic settlement. Using xenPlatform on day 1 adds sub-merchant KYC/onboarding overhead the MVP doesn't need — all money is the platform owner's in MVP, so no split is required.

**Addendum — payment-gateway seam, 2026-07-23:** Xendit requires business-credential/KYC verification before approving an account, and approval isn't guaranteed — if Xendit rejects the platform's business verification, a fallback gateway with a sub-account/split-payment feature comparable to xenPlatform would be needed (that feature, not just "any gateway," is the actual requirement driving the fallback candidate list). Unlike the Supplier situation (ADR-006), no second payment gateway is confirmed or researched yet, so building a second full implementation now would be guessing at an unconfirmed shape. Instead: build directly against Xendit's Payment Request API, but behind a **thin** `PaymentGateway` interface (`createPayment()`, `getPayment()`, `verifyWebhookSignature()`, `parseWebhookEvent()` — see `app/Services/Payment/`) so that *if* a swap is ever needed, it costs one new adapter implementation, not a rewrite of Order/Ledger business logic. This is a smaller, cheaper seam than the Supplier Adapter (4 methods vs. 5, no capability-flag complexity) precisely because — unlike suppliers — only one gateway is ever actually in use at a time; the interface exists purely to isolate switching risk, not to run multiple gateways concurrently. Does not change the MVP decision above (Xendit only, xenPlatform deferred) — it only changes how the Xendit integration is wired internally.

**Addendum — xenPlatform sub-account type: OWNED, not MANAGED, 2026-07-24:** researched directly against Xendit's docs (docs.xendit.co/xenplatform/accounts, help.xendit.co) before this decision, not assumed. xenPlatform has two sub-account types with materially different reseller-facing behavior:
- **MANAGED** — the partner (reseller) registers via an invitation email, gets their own real Xendit dashboard login, completes their own onboarding/KYC, and can add their own bank account and withdraw directly through Xendit's own UI, potentially bypassing our Admin Panel entirely for that action.
- **OWNED** — sub-accounts are invisible to partners and fully controlled by the platform ("department store" model — the customer, and here the *reseller*, only ever sees the platform, never Xendit). Minimal KYC. Critically, Xendit has no feature for an OWNED sub-account to register its own withdrawal bank account — payout is pushed by the **Master Account** (us) via the Disbursement/Payout API using a `for-user-id` header identifying the sub-account, or via Batch Disbursement from the Master Account's own dashboard.

**Decision:** Phase 2 reseller sub-accounts will be **OWNED**, not MANAGED. Founder requirement: resellers must never be aware Xendit is the underlying processor — the platform is the only party they interact with for payouts, full stop. MANAGED directly breaks this (separate Xendit login, Xendit-branded dashboard). OWNED matches it exactly — Xendit is invisible to the reseller by design.

**Consequence to track:** because OWNED sub-accounts don't store their own withdrawal bank account with Xendit, the platform must supply the destination bank account on every Disbursement API call. This means the `Withdrawal` model's `bank_name`/`bank_account_no`/`bank_account_holder` fields (built this session for the MVP platform-owner withdrawal flow, WTH-1..5) are **already the right shape for Phase 2** — no rework needed there. The existing Admin Panel approve/reject/complete workflow also carries forward as the reseller-facing "payout" experience: Phase 2 only needs to swap the `complete` action's "admin marks it done after transferring manually" step for "a real Disbursement API call, `for-user-id` = the reseller's sub-account ID" — the reseller still only ever sees our Admin Panel's status, never Xendit's. Also unverified and worth confirming directly with Xendit before Phase 2 build starts, not assumed from documentation research alone: OWNED sub-accounts are reported as disabled by default for Indonesia-based accounts — Malaysia availability wasn't confirmed in this research pass.

**Addendum — multi-gateway seam widened, 2026-07-25:** founder flagged that Xendit's real fee rates (discovered while building the Payment Methods tool, see docs/prd.md §14) are high enough that a gateway swap or running two gateways concurrently side-by-side (not just a one-time future swap) is now a real possibility, not a hypothetical "if Xendit rejects KYC" scenario. This changes the 2026-07-23 addendum's founding assumption ("only one gateway is ever actually in use at a time") — but the fix applied is still schema/plumbing readiness only, **not** a second gateway implementation, for the same reason ADR-006 gives for suppliers: no second gateway is researched or confirmed yet, so building one now would be guessing at an unconfirmed shape.

What changed: `payment_methods` (the SET-7/SET-11 admin tool) gained a `gateway` column — every channel now carries which gateway owns it, not just its fee rate. `CheckoutService::initiate()` no longer constructor-injects one fixed `PaymentGateway`; it takes the resolved gateway as a method parameter instead, so a single checkout can route different channels to different gateways without touching pricing/ledger/order logic at all. A new `PaymentGatewayFactory` resolves an implementation by name through the container (`payment-gateway.<name>` binding keys), throwing `UnsupportedPaymentGatewayException` for anything not registered — today that's every name except `'xendit'`. `PaymentGateway::class`'s own default binding stays Xendit-only, since the webhook route (`/api/webhooks/xendit`) is inherently gateway-specific by URL and doesn't need per-request resolution.

**Consequence to track:** when a second gateway is actually chosen and researched, it costs exactly one new adapter (implementing `PaymentGateway`) plus one new `payment-gateway.<name>` container binding plus admin flipping the right `payment_methods.gateway` values — no changes to `CheckoutController`, `CheckoutService`, the Order model, or the ledger. The webhook side is the one place that *does* need new code per gateway: each gateway's callback verification/parsing is different enough (Xendit's is a plain token comparison, not HMAC) that it gets its own controller + route, mirroring how `XenditWebhookController` is Xendit-specific today, not a shared abstraction.

**Addendum — `customer` object required, fixed and verified live, 2026-07-25 (same session):** the Payment Methods "Test" action (built earlier this same session) immediately surfaced a real gap: Xendit's Payment Request API requires exactly one of `customer`/`customer_id` for at least the FPX channel — confusingly worded as "Only one of 'customer' or 'customer_id' should be present" even when *neither* was sent (a `oneOf`-style JSON Schema validator's generic message, confirmed by re-checking docs.xendit.co/apidocs/create-payment-request). Guest checkout never collected a customer name, only email/phone/player_id, so this required a small, deliberate product decision, not just a code fix: founder chose to **add a real `customer_name` field to checkout** (not a placeholder derived from email) — see the create Order migration and `CreateCheckoutRequest` for where it landed. New `App\Services\Payment\PaymentCustomer` DTO carries `referenceId`/`givenNames`/`email`/`mobileNumber` into `XenditGateway::createPayment()`'s `customer` object (`type: INDIVIDUAL`, matching Xendit's real schema). **Verified live against the real Xendit sandbox** via the Payment Methods "Test" action: `AMBANK_FPX` and `GRABPAY` both now return `last_test_result: "success"` (previously the `customer`/`customer_id` failure) — not just unit-tested against a mock. `CARDS` still fails (needs `channel_properties.card_details`, a separate, expected gap — card entry happens via Xendit-hosted fields per PAY-4, not something the Payment Methods tool itself should supply).

## ADR-002 (D2): Ledger-based balance, not a mutable column

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-23

**Decision:** Every credit/debit (order profit, withdrawal, voucher issuance) is written as an immutable `LedgerEntry` row. Current balance for any owner (platform or, in Phase 2, reseller) is always `SUM(ledger entries)` — never a `balance` column that gets directly `UPDATE`d.

**Rationale:** A mutable `balance` column is vulnerable to race conditions — e.g. two concurrent withdrawal requests both reading the same starting balance before either write completes, resulting in double payout. A ledger also gives a full, queryable audit trail for financial disputes ("why is the balance what it is?" is always answerable).

**Addendum — implementation, 2026-07-23:** `SELECT SUM(...) FOR UPDATE` on `ledger_entries` alone can't serialize concurrent withdrawals reliably: a brand-new owner has zero existing rows to lock, so two first-ever withdrawals could both pass the sufficiency check before either commits. Solved with a second table, `ledger_accounts` — one row per owner, created upfront, holding **no balance data at all**, existing purely as a lock anchor. `LedgerService::withdraw()` runs inside a DB transaction that `lockForUpdate()`s this row before computing `SUM(ledger_entries)` and checking sufficiency, so a second concurrent withdrawal attempt blocks until the first commits. Verified with a real two-OS-process test (`tests/Concurrency/LedgerWithdrawConcurrencyTest.php`, run via `phpunit.concurrency.xml` against the dockerized MySQL in `docker-compose.yml` — SQLite's file-level locking can't faithfully exercise this, so the default `:memory:` test suite doesn't cover this specific guarantee). This does not weaken the "no mutable balance column" principle above: `ledger_accounts` never stores an amount, only `ledger_entries` does.

## ADR-003 (D3): Tenant-aware schema, platform-owner-only MVP features

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-23

**Decision:** Schema and query layer are built multi-tenant-aware from day 1 (`reseller_id` as a first-class column, tenant scoping enforced via ORM global scopes, not per-query convention). MVP *feature* scope, however, is platform-owner-only — no reseller self-service dashboard, no custom domains, no reseller onboarding flow.

**Rationale:** Retrofitting tenant isolation onto a single-tenant schema after real data exists is expensive and risky — a single missed `WHERE` clause becomes a cross-tenant data leak. Architecture readiness is cheap now; reseller-facing *features* are expensive and can be deferred without penalty. This separates the cheap decision (schema shape) from the expensive one (build reseller UX).

## ADR-004 (D4): No cash refunds, ever

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-23

**Decision:** Failed or undeliverable orders are resolved by (a) retry delivery, or (b) issuing a Voucher (store credit) — never a refund back to the original payment method.

**Rationale:** Eliminates an entire class of payment-gateway refund-API integration risk (partial refunds, reconciliation) and closes a common cash-out fraud vector (stolen-card fraud can't be laundered into cash back via a refund). Directly reinforced by ADR-005.

---

## ADR-005 (D5): Player-ID pre-payment validation is not universal

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-23

**Decision:** The order flow must support two paths: validate-before-payment where the supplier/game supports a dedicated validation endpoint, and payment-then-validate-at-order-time as a fallback where it doesn't.

**Rationale:** Confirmed via direct research on real supplier APIs that dedicated validate-ID endpoints are typically only available for specific games (e.g. MLBB), not universally offered by every supplier for every game. This cannot be engineered around — for suppliers without pre-validation, "customer pays, then player ID turns out invalid" is a real scenario that must be handled by policy (ADR-004's voucher-only refund), not assumed away by code.

**Addendum, 2026-07-25 — Gamevion re-confirmed against the live spec, and a related gap surfaced:** re-checked directly against `docs.gamevion.com/gamevion-api` (v1.0.10, fetched live, not recalled from memory) in response to a founder question. Gamevion's entire API surface is exactly 4 endpoints — `check-balance`, `product`, `order`, `check-status` — **zero validation endpoints, for any game, not just "not universal."** `GamevionAdapter::validatePlayer()` throwing `ValidationNotSupportedException` unconditionally is confirmed correct, not a stale assumption.

The same check surfaced a related, previously-undocumented gap: `POST /api/order`'s `data` field is a single opaque **string** (e.g. `"123456|1234"`) — Gamevion's API has no concept of structured per-product input fields either (no schema telling us "this game needs player_id + server_id, this one needs only player_id"). That knowledge has to live entirely on our side. The schema already has a home for it (`Game.validation_rules`, JSON — see `prd.md` §8), but no admin UI to populate it and no `CheckoutService`/`OrderFulfillmentService` logic yet to assemble the `data` string from it. Not built as of this addendum — tracked in `prd.md` §14's NEXT SESSION pointer.

**Addendum, 2026-07-25 (new session) — independent third-party MLBB player-ID validators, built:** since Gamevion itself has zero validation endpoints (confirmed above), the founder separately researched **unofficial, reverse-engineered validate-ID endpoints from three existing MLBB top-up storefronts** — AcidGameShop, Nexone.ph, and MooGold — none of which are Gamevion or any of our own suppliers; this is a wholly independent signal source, not a supplier capability. All three were live-tested (valid and invalid cases) with a real MLBB Malaysia account before any code was written:

- **AcidGameShop** (`POST /api/validate-mlbb`) — cleanest: stateless JSON in/out, `400` + `{"error":...}` on invalid.
- **Nexone.ph** (`POST /pages/get_check_id`) — session-bound: requires first `GET /idchecker` to scrape a one-time `checkToken` tied to that request's cookies, replayed on the actual check. Always returns HTTP `200`; validity is `success: true/false` in the body.
- **MooGold** (a WooCommerce `id-validation-new` plugin endpoint) — most fragile: no structured fields, everything in a free-text `message` string; confirmed live that `icon` stays `"success"` even on a confirmed-invalid ID (`status` is the only real validity flag) and that the `Country` line is sometimes absent even for the identical valid account on a repeat call.

**Decision:** a fallback chain, priority **AcidGameShop → Nexone.ph → MooGold** (founder's own reliability ranking), each behind a common `PlayerValidator` interface (`app/Services/PlayerValidation/`) normalizing to `{valid, nickname, countryCode, provider}` — same normalizer discipline as `SupplierAdapter`/`SupplierResponse` (ADAPT-2). Country is canonicalized by **decoding the flag emoji into its ISO alpha-2 code algorithmically** (a flag emoji is exactly two Unicode Regional Indicator Symbols, one per letter) rather than a country-name lookup table, since it's the one signal both AcidGameShop and Nexone carry consistently; MooGold carries neither reliably, so `countryCode` normalizes to `null` there — a real, distinct "region unknown" outcome, never conflated with "invalid".

**Founder correction, same session — validator is a first-class admin entity, not a string tag:** the first cut put a raw, free-typed `validator_key` string directly on `Game`/`player_region_mappings`. The founder caught the real gap this leaves: nothing stops an admin typing a key with no real backend implementation, and nothing surfaces whether a configured key is actually working. Restructured to a real `PlayerValidatorProfile` model (`player_validator_profiles` table — `name`, `key`, `last_tested_at`, `last_test_result`), with `key` constrained (`Rule::in`) to `PlayerValidatorRegistry::AVAILABLE_KEYS` — the finite set of keys with a real container binding — so a profile can never be created pointing at nothing. A live **"Test this validator"** action (admin supplies a real Player ID/Server ID) runs the actual chain and reports `UnsupportedPlayerValidatorException` (key not bound at all) vs. a genuine result — proving the validator is plugged in, not just configured. `player_region_mappings` (MUI-5's "region-based game routing rules" — which of our own Game rows a given country must buy from, since no provider knows our catalog) now nests under `player_validator_profile_id`, not a loose string, and `games.player_validator_profile_id`/`player_validator_enabled` (nullable FK + kill-switch) replace the original string field. Built and shipped: the middleware Validators screen (MUI-5), the `PlayerValidator` chain + registry, all schema, 33+ tests.

**Addendum, 2026-07-26 (new session) — toggle, public endpoint, and storefront flow all built and live-verified:** the three items this addendum previously flagged as "not yet built" are now two-thirds done. `/admin/games` gained the "Requires Player Validation" toggle (profile picker + on/off, writing `player_validator_profile_id`/`player_validator_enabled` — `UpdateGameRequest` previously silently dropped both fields even if sent). `POST /api/games/{game}/validate-player` (public, no auth, per ADR-011) resolves the profile, runs the chain, maps country against `player_region_mappings`, and returns one of `invalid`/`region_unknown`/`wrong_region`/`valid` — the first thing that ever writes a `player_validations` row. The storefront (`storefront/`, scaffolded this same session — see ADR-009's own addendum) wires this into `/order/[slug]`'s wizard Step 1. **Still not built**: `CheckoutController` server-side enforcement — the storefront gates its own "Proceed to Payment" client-side, but nothing re-checks `player_validations` on the actual `POST /api/checkout` call yet, so a direct API call still bypasses it. See `prd.md` §14's newest NEXT SESSION pointer.

**Still separate, still unconfirmed:** this new validator layer answers "is this MLBB account's region known" — it does **not** resolve Gamevion's own still-open question (this ADR's first addendum, and ADR-006's newest addendum) of how an invalid player/server ID actually surfaces when Gamevion processes a real order. The two are unrelated mechanisms; don't conflate a "yes" on one as progress on the other.

## ADR-006 (D6): Supplier Adapter/Normalizer layer is MVP, not Phase 2

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-23 (supersedes the original PRD v0.2 draft, which listed a "Custom Supplier Adapter SDK" as a Phase 2 / future-phase item)

**Decision:** Every supplier integration is implemented behind a common internal interface. Business logic never reads a raw supplier response directly — every adapter normalizes into one canonical internal shape.

**Rationale:** Comparing two real supplier APIs during the foundation audit (Gamevion API docs; a second store's MLBB-validator endpoints) showed materially different auth schemes, response envelopes, and error shapes even between just two suppliers. Without a normalizing layer from day 1, every new supplier integration touches business logic directly, and inconsistent error handling across suppliers becomes a direct source of financial/logic bugs.

**Addendum — shared outbound proxy seam, 2026-07-25:** some suppliers require the *calling* party's IP to be whitelisted before their API accepts requests at all — a constraint that has nothing to do with Adapter normalization, but does affect how an Adapter's HTTP client is constructed. Confirmed (by reading Gamevion's own API docs directly) that Gamevion itself does **not** require IP whitelisting — auth is Bearer + `X-API-KEY` only, no network-level restriction. This addendum exists for the *next* supplier that does. Rather than let each Adapter invent its own proxy handling, `config/services.php['proxy']` (`SUPPLIER_PROXY_ENABLED`/`SUPPLIER_PROXY_URL`) is one shared, generic outbound-proxy config any Adapter can accept as an optional constructor argument (see `GamevionAdapter`'s `proxyUrl` param) — one proxy/static-IP covers every supplier that needs whitelisting, since the whitelisting party only cares which IP the request came from, not what else that IP is also used for. Only build a second proxy if a future supplier demands an exclusive or region-specific IP. The proxy credential itself follows the same handling as every other supplier secret in this codebase (§7 of `foundation-security.md`): env-only, never committed, not yet moved to `Supplier.api_config` (SUPP-5) pending that table's real wiring.

**Addendum — first real end-to-end order + two live findings, 2026-07-25 (same session as the payment `customer` fix):** ran the platform's first-ever real checkout → payment → webhook → Gamevion fulfillment chain for a real order (MLBB Malaysia, "13 + 1 Diamonds", real User ID/Server ID supplied by the founder), Xendit in real sandbox mode, Gamevion with `GAMEVION_SANDBOX=true`. Found and fixed one real adapter bug, and isolated (but did not fix — not ours to fix) one real Gamevion-side sandbox limitation:
1. **[Fixed] `GamevionAdapter`'s `telp` field rejects a leading `+`.** Gamevion's own error — `"telp field must be between 9 and 13 digits"` — was returned for `"+60123456789"`, which *is* 11 digits; their validator fails entirely on the non-digit `+` character rather than counting digits only. `GamevionAdapter::normalizePhone()` now strips every non-digit character before sending `telp`, matching ADAPT-4's existing principle (the Adapter absorbs a supplier's specific format quirks, business logic never needs to know). Confirmed fixed live: same order retried post-fix produced no `telp` error at all.
2. **[Isolated, not ours to fix] Gamevion's sandbox `/api/order` returns a generic `{"error":true,"code":500,"message":"Server error"}` for any real, valid `product_code` — while the exact same request against Gamevion's real docs example values (`referenceNumber` formatted `GV-...`, a placeholder `product_code`) correctly returns `422` "product code invalid".** Ruled out, methodically, before concluding this: not `telp` format (fixed and confirmed working), not `referenceNumber` format (`GV-` prefix vs. our own `REF-` prefix made no difference), not product-specific (both a Free Fire item and an MLBB item — two different products — hit the identical `500`). **Conclusively isolated by switching the same adapter to `sandbox: false` (production) with the same real product code and request shape**: production returned a clean `400 Insufficient balance` (the account's real production balance is confirmed `0`, so this is the correct, expected response, not a lucky success) — proving the request itself is well-formed and Gamevion's production order-processing pipeline handles it correctly. The sandbox-mode failure is therefore Gamevion's own sandbox environment, not our adapter or request shape. **Action:** report this to Gamevion support with the diagnostic evidence above (fake product → clean `422`; real product → `500` in sandbox only, `400` in production) — not a code task for this codebase.

**Consequence to track:** the platform's checkout→payment→fulfillment chain is now proven correct end-to-end for the payment half (real `201` from Xendit, real webhook processed, `payment_status` correctly reaches `paid`). The delivery half is blocked purely on Gamevion's sandbox environment being unable to complete a real order right now — re-attempt once Gamevion support resolves it, or accept `GAMEVION_SANDBOX=false` for real fulfillment testing once the account has real balance (not recommended casually, since that spends real money and delivers to a real player account).

**Addendum — no sandbox `product_code` exists that can successfully order, 2026-07-25 (follow-up same day):** re-verified the sandbox `500` above is still live today, and closed out the obvious next question — "is there a sandbox-specific product code that avoids it?" Checked directly against the local copy of Gamevion's OAS spec (`gamevion-api.json`, v1.0.10): `/api/order`'s `product_code` schema has no relationship to `/api/product`'s `sandbox` body flag — they're two independent mechanisms that only *look* connected. Confirmed live with raw request/response evidence:
1. `POST /api/product` with `{"sandbox": true}` returns `{"error":false,"code":200,"message":"Products Simulation (Sandbox)","data":[{"sandbox_code":"234","sandbox_serviceName":"mlbb5","sandbox_category":"Mobile Legends","sandbox_price":"1000.00","sandbox_status":"active"}]}` — Gamevion's own `message` field literally calls this "Simulation," and it's a single hardcoded entry, not a real catalog.
2. Feeding that `sandbox_code` (`234`) into `POST /api/order` as `product_code` (with the founder-supplied test IDs, `data: "51049607|2005"`) returns a clean `{"error":true,"code":422,"message":"The selected product code is invalid."}` — Gamevion's order endpoint validates `product_code` against the **real production catalog**, not the sandbox-simulation list, so a `sandbox_code` value is never valid there.
3. Re-tested a real production code (`GV572`, "13 + 1 Diamonds," the same MLBB item from the addendum above) under `X-ENVIRONMENT: sandbox` with the same test IDs — reproduced the identical `{"error":true,"code":500,"message":"Server error"}`, confirming the bug is still present, not a one-off.

**Net conclusion: there is currently no `product_code` — sandbox-simulation or real — that can complete a successful order through Gamevion's sandbox mode.** Simulation codes are rejected as invalid (`422`); real codes hit Gamevion's server bug (`500`). This doesn't change the action from the addendum above (report to Gamevion support; the `422`/`500`/`400` evidence trail across sandbox and production is the diagnostic package to send them).

**Open question surfaced, not yet investigated:** Gamevion has no player-validation endpoint (ADR-005) — player/server ID correctness is only checked implicitly, inside order processing itself. Every real-product order attempt so far has been stopped earlier (by the sandbox `500` here, or by `400 Insufficient balance` in production) before reaching that implicit check, so it's still unconfirmed whether a given `playerId`/`serverId` pair (e.g. the founder-supplied `51049607`/`2005`) is actually valid from Gamevion's side. Tracked for a follow-up session — needs its own investigation into what "player ID validation" can mean with no dedicated endpoint (e.g. whether topping up production balance and letting a real order run is the only way to observe it).

## ADR-007 (D7): Internal fraud blacklist is first-class MVP

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-23

**Decision:** The system maintains its own internal blacklist of player IDs and/or customer contacts, checked at order creation — independent of whatever blacklist (if any) a given supplier offers.

**Rationale:** Observed in a real competitor's API integration (a `check-blacklist` endpoint). The platform should not depend on a supplier providing this protection — it must be built and owned internally, populated from the platform's own chargeback/fraud history.

---

## ADR-008 (D8): Split frontend stack — Vue for Admin, Next.js for Storefront

**Status:** ~~Accepted~~ **Superseded by ADR-009** — 2026-07-23 (same-day reversal, before any code was written)

**Decision:** Admin Panel is a Vue 3 + Vite SPA. Storefront is Next.js (React). This is a deliberate two-ecosystem split, not a single unified frontend framework.

**Rationale:** Admin Panel has no SEO/SSR requirement (it's behind auth, never indexed) — a plain Vue 3 SPA matches the legacy system's precedent and keeps things simple. Storefront has a genuine SEO/SSR requirement (see PRD §6.16 — meta tags, OG images, per-game SEO exist specifically to drive organic traffic), which a plain client-rendered SPA serves poorly. The team chose Next.js over the Vue-ecosystem alternative (Nuxt 3) specifically for React's larger ecosystem and Next.js's SSR maturity, consciously accepting the cost of maintaining two frontend stacks instead of one.

**Why superseded:** the "matches legacy precedent" argument only carries weight if the team is actually going to reference/maintain the legacy Vue codebase directly — for a greenfield build by a team that already prefers React (as evidenced by choosing Next.js over Nuxt for the Storefront in this same decision), keeping Vue for Admin only adds a second framework to learn and maintain, with no offsetting benefit. See ADR-009.

---

## ADR-009 (D8-revised): Unify frontend stack — Next.js (React) for both Admin Panel and Storefront

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-23 — supersedes ADR-008

**Decision:** Both Admin Panel and Storefront are built in Next.js (React), under Laravel's REST API. Admin Panel uses Next.js in a client-rendered/SPA-style mode (`"use client"` throughout, no server-side data fetching through Next) — it calls the Laravel API directly from the browser using the Bearer token (AUTH-2), the same way the Storefront's dynamic/authenticated parts would. Next's SSR/React Server Components are used only where the Storefront actually benefits from them (public, SEO-relevant pages).

**Rationale:** Once the team confirmed a genuine preference for React over Vue (ADR-008's own storefront decision), maintaining Vue for Admin Panel purely for "legacy precedent" cost more (a second framework, second tooling/testing/CI setup, no shared component/utility code between the two apps) than it saved. A single stack means one set of conventions, and a shared API-client/types layer between Admin and Storefront. Admin Panel gains nothing from SSR (it's behind auth, never indexed), so it deliberately avoids the added complexity of Next's server/client component boundary — treat it as "a SPA that happens to run on Next.js," not a server-rendered app.

**Consequence to track:** because Admin Panel doesn't need Next's SSR features, watch for accidental complexity creep (e.g. someone reaching for a Server Component or a Next API route for something that's simpler as a plain client fetch to Laravel) — if that starts happening often, it's a signal Admin Panel would genuinely be simpler as a plain Vite + React SPA instead of Next.js. Not a concern to solve now, just one to notice later.

**Addendum, 2026-07-26 (new session) — Storefront actually scaffolded, and a page-count decision worth recording:** `storefront/` now exists (Next.js 16, mirrors `admin/`'s `apiFetch` pattern, own design system — see `prd.md` §14's Storefront app row for the full build). One real decision made while reconciling the founder's own HTML page references against this project's real backend: the founder's 3 reference pages (top-up wizard / order-review / order-status) were built as 2 real routes, not 3 — `OrderForm` already holds all wizard state client-side (unlike 3 static HTML files, which had to pass state through URL querystrings between page loads), so "Order Review" became a **Review Modal** opened from `/order/[slug]` rather than a separate route, and `/order/status/[orderNumber]` is shared by both the post-checkout redirect and `/track-order`'s lookup result (one tracker component, two entry points — the founder's own steer, not assumed). Kept SSR/RSC usage minimal even on the founder-approved homepage redesign — this is a transactional/checkout-adjacent app, not marketing-only, so most pages still lean on client interactivity (wizard state, live polling) rather than server-rendered content.

## ADR-010: Docker for MySQL only, not full Laravel Sail

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-23

**Decision:** `backend/docker-compose.yml` runs a single MySQL 8.4 service, nothing else. PHP continues to run natively via Laravel Herd (already working). A dedicated PHPUnit config, `phpunit.concurrency.xml`, points only the small set of tests that need real row-level locking at this dockerized MySQL; the default `phpunit.xml` suite keeps using sqlite `:memory:` for speed.

**Rationale:** SQLite locks at the file level, not per-row, so it can't faithfully prove the ledger/voucher locking guarantees (ADR-002 addendum) — those specific tests need real MySQL `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` semantics. Laravel Sail was considered but rejected for this stage: Sail also containerizes PHP, which would duplicate/conflict with the already-working native Herd setup for no added benefit — the only real gap was "we have no database server," not "we need a full containerized stack." Keeping Docker's footprint to just the one MySQL service is the minimal fix for the actual gap.

**Consequence to track:** concurrency-sensitive tests live in `tests/Concurrency/` and require `docker compose up -d` first; they are intentionally excluded from the default `php artisan test` run so day-to-day development never depends on Docker being up. Revisit if/when the project needs Sail's broader containerization (e.g. matching a containerized production deploy) — not needed for MVP.

---

## ADR-011: Storefront stays guest-checkout — no Customer account/auth in MVP

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-24

**Decision:** The storefront has no customer login/registration and no `Customer` table. A purchase only ever captures `customer_email`/`customer_phone` as plain strings on the `Order` row itself — there is no persistent customer identity anywhere in the system. Auth (Sanctum) exists only for `AdminUser` (Super Admin/Admin).

**Rationale:** Confirmed via live comparison of two real reference sites: keroxshop.com (our own current storefront) has no login/register anywhere — only a "Track Order" page that looks up status by order number, which is exactly the guest-checkout + reference-lookup model already assumed in the PRD's data model (no Customer entity was ever listed in §8). gamevion.com, by contrast, does have full customer accounts — but for a reason specific to its own business model, not applicable here: it runs a pre-funded customer wallet ("Top Up" your own balance, then spend it) plus a reseller/membership-tier program where customers can upgrade and refer others. Both of those features genuinely require persistent identity. Neither exists in this PRD's MVP scope — there is no customer wallet, and Phase 2's reseller concept is a business owner with their own storefront, not a walk-in customer upgrading their tier. Since the actual driver behind Gamevion's account requirement doesn't apply here, adopting accounts anyway would be copying a competitor's architecture without its underlying reason.

**Consequence to track:** if a customer-facing wallet, loyalty program, or persistent order-history feature is ever deliberately added later, it changes this decision and deserves its own ADR entry (per this file's own convention — supersede, don't silently rewrite). Until then, do not add a `Customer` model, customer login endpoints, or a `customer_id` foreign key "just in case" — `Order.customer_email` is sufficient for the guest-checkout model this ADR commits to.

## ADR-012: Admin Panel UI built on the free TailAdmin template as a component/layout reference

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-24

**Decision:** The Admin Panel's visual layer (sidebar, header, tables, badges, buttons, modals, dropdowns, Tailwind v4 theme tokens) is built by porting and trimming components from the free, MIT-licensed TailAdmin Next.js dashboard template, rather than designing a component system from scratch or adopting a full component library (shadcn/ui, MUI, etc.). Only components an actual screen uses get ported in — the template's calendar, charts, carousel, and other unused pieces are left behind, not brought in speculatively.

**Rationale:** ADR-009 already committed the Admin Panel to a client-rendered Next.js SPA; TailAdmin is itself a Next.js App Router template on the same stack (Next 16, React 19, Tailwind v4), and the components actually used (Table/Badge/Button/Modal/Dropdown) are pure React + Tailwind with zero external runtime dependencies — porting them costs no new npm packages. The template ships **zero business logic and zero data-fetching**: every page/component hardcodes its own inline mock data array, with no API abstraction, loading, or error states anywhere. That's treated as a feature, not a gap — there's no wrong data-layer pattern baked in to fight against, only visual/structural components to reuse.

**Build approach this implies:** wire per-feature, not "build the whole UI as a mockup, then wire everything to the backend afterward." For each screen: adopt the template's UI shell, define the TypeScript data contract the screen needs, then wire it to the real backend endpoint in the same pass whenever that endpoint already exists or is simple to add — as done for AUTH-4 (Admin Users list/create/edit/status), the first full vertical slice built this way. Only stub with placeholder data when the backend shape is still genuinely undecided (e.g. Dashboard KPI aggregation queries not yet designed), and swap it for the real fetch before moving to the next screen — never as a separate later "wiring phase."

**Consequence to track:** TailAdmin's own source lives outside this repo (on the founder's machine) and is a **UI/UX reference only** — its business data, feature-completeness claims, and any "Pro"-tier upsell content are not part of this project, the same "reference, not fact" discipline applied to the legacy KeroxShop walkthrough in [`legacy-reference-notes.md`](./legacy-reference-notes.md). Copy component shape and interaction patterns; never copy business assumptions.

## ADR-013: Platform owner is the first Reseller row, not a parallel single-tenant concept

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-25 (formalizes a decision discussed but not previously written down; surfaced as a documentation gap during the CheckoutController planning pass)

**Decision:** There is no separate "platform owner" concept modeled alongside `Reseller`. The platform owner *is* the first `Reseller` row (`business_name = 'Platform Owner'`, `markup_pct = 0`), created once (seeded in `DatabaseSeeder`, with a `firstOrCreate` safety net in `CheckoutController` for any environment that skipped seeding). Every Order's `reseller_id`, and both `LedgerEntry` rows a delivered order writes (platform + reseller profit), reference this same row in MVP.

**Rationale:** This was already implied by `prd.md` §8's own Reseller data-model row ("Table exists from MVP... exactly one row is created for the platform owner's own internal storefront, typically with `markup_pct = 0`, so the pricing/ledger formulas never special-case 'no reseller yet'") and by ADR-003's tenant-ready-schema-from-day-1 decision — but the table was never actually built, and the *why* (avoid a parallel single-tenant code path that Phase 2 would have to delete) was never captured as its own decision. Making it explicit now: `PricingService::calculate()` always takes a `resellerMarkupPct`; `OrderFulfillmentService::creditProfit()` always writes two ledger entries (platform + reseller). Neither has an "if no reseller yet" branch — MVP and Phase 2 run the exact same code path, just against more `Reseller` rows.

**Consequence to track:** `CheckoutController` resolving `Reseller::firstOrCreate(['business_name' => 'Platform Owner'], ...)` is a stopgap for "exactly one MVP reseller," not a pattern to repeat once Phase 2 onboards real resellers — at that point, checkout needs a real reseller-resolution strategy (subdomain/custom-domain routing, per ADR's own open question in `prd.md` §12), and this hardcoded lookup gets replaced, not extended.

## ADR-014: 24/7 burst-resilience baseline — queue, retry, indexing, caching, rate-limiting, observability

**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-26 (design session while blocked on Gamevion support's reply re: ADR-006's sandbox `500`; founder explicitly asked to strengthen the foundation in parallel rather than wait idle)

**Context:** A read-only audit of the live codebase (not assumption) found the money-critical path had zero protection against exactly the failure modes a 24/7 top-up storefront with bursty concurrent traffic will hit: `XenditWebhookController::handle()` calls `OrderFulfillmentService::fulfill()` — which makes a live Gamevion HTTP call — **synchronously inside the webhook request**, while holding `fulfill()`'s own row lock (added in the 2026-07-24 security review); `orders.payment_ref`, the exact column every webhook looks up by, has **no index**; outbound calls to Xendit/Gamevion have **no retry** on transient failure; there is **no caching** anywhere (`grep Cache::` returns zero hits); there is **no rate-limiting** on any route (`grep throttle` returns zero hits) — `POST /api/checkout` and the webhook endpoint are both wide open; and there is no error-tracking/health-check beyond Laravel's default file log. Full findings are in the session transcript, not duplicated here.

**Decision (per sub-area, each grilled with the founder one at a time before being accepted):**

1. **Queue** — introduce a `database`-driver queue (the `jobs` table already exists from the Laravel scaffold, unused until now — zero new infra). `XenditWebhookController` becomes thin: verify signature → update `payment_status` → `dispatch(new FulfillOrderJob($order))` → ack. `OrderFulfillmentService`'s own interface and its `lockForUpdate()` guard are untouched — only *where* it's called from moves. Redis is deferred until real traffic actually justifies the extra infra/ops burden; this project currently has no production infra defined at all (`backend/docker-compose.yml` is MySQL-for-testing only).
2. **Retry (network)** — add `->retry(3, [200, 500, 1000])`-shaped backoff to `GamevionAdapter`/`XenditGateway`'s shared `client()`, scoped to transient failures (timeout/5xx) only — a 4xx like `422 invalid product code` (the exact error ADR-006's sandbox retest just reproduced) must never be retried, since retrying a validation error just wastes the budget and delays the real failure signal.
3. **Retry (business)** — `FulfillOrderJob` gets its own `$tries`/`backoff()` aligned with #2. When exhausted, the order lands at `delivery_status: failed` for admin review — same terminal state `OrderFulfillmentService` already produces today, just reached after automated retry instead of on the first blip. Exposing a manual retry from `/admin/orders` (ORD-7, already tracked as unbuilt in `prd.md` §14/§15) becomes part of this same effort rather than a separate later pass, since a queued job without an operator-visible retry path is a worse UX than the current synchronous one.
4. **Database indexing** — add an index on `orders.payment_ref` (every webhook's lookup column, currently unindexed — the single highest-impact fix found) and a composite index on `orders(payment_status, delivery_status)` (the Admin Orders `need_action`/`processing`/`completed` filters, per `OrderController`). Pure migration work, no interface change, no founder trade-off — proceeding without a grill question.
5. **Caching** — `Cache::remember()` (TTL 60s) on read-heavy, admin-curated listings only (Games/Packages, Payment Methods) with **invalidate-on-write**: any admin action that changes a cached row (status toggle, markup/fee update) clears that cache key immediately rather than waiting out the TTL, so a customer is never shown a stale toggle for more than a moment. **Explicitly out of scope: pricing/checkout calculation itself** — `PricingService`/`CheckoutTotalService`/`CheckoutService::initiate()` keep reading live from the DB, unchanged. This preserves ORD-9's existing "money is snapshotted at checkout time from a live source, never from a stale intermediate copy" discipline; caching is a read-listing optimization, not a money-path optimization, and the two must never blur.
6. **Observability** — founder chose to **stay on file-based logging for now, no external error-tracking service** (Sentry etc. explicitly declined — cost/data-residency judged not worth it before real production traffic exists). What *is* being added: consistent structured log context (`order_number`/`reference_number` attached to every log line on the fulfillment/payment path, not just ad-hoc `Log::warning()` calls as today), a `GET /api/health` endpoint (DB + queue connection check), and `throttle:10,1` on `POST /api/checkout` (10 requests/minute/IP — chosen loose enough not to block a genuine customer retrying after a failed attempt, tight enough to blunt a flood). The Xendit webhook route is deliberately **not** IP-rate-limited the same way — `x-callback-token` verification is already its auth boundary, and by-IP throttling risks blocking Xendit's own retry infrastructure, which shares egress IPs across their customers.
7. **Load balancing** — deferred, no code change now. Recorded only because the audit confirmed the codebase is *already* positioned for it whenever it's needed: auth is Bearer-token (Sanctum), not cookie/session-affinity-based, and `SESSION_DRIVER`/`CACHE_STORE` both already default to `database`, not `file` — so horizontal scaling later needs new infra, not a rewrite of how state is held.

**Rationale:** Every sub-area above was scoped to change an implementation, not an interface — `SupplierAdapter`, `PaymentGateway`, and `OrderFulfillmentService`'s public contracts are untouched by #1–#3; this is the same "deepen the module, don't reshape its seam" discipline the codebase already follows for the Adapter/Gateway layer (ADR-001, ADR-006), applied to resilience concerns instead of business features.

**Consequence to track:** this ADR records *design intent*, agreed before implementation started (per the founder's explicit request — plan and review first). Update `prd.md` §14/§15 as each numbered item actually ships; do not treat this entry as proof any of it is built yet.
